title: How Long Would You Last on Every Planet?
note: Part 1 of the video: the first three minutes (Mercury, Venus, Mars). gap = seconds of silence after the line.

lines.text: Mercury.
Mercury is the closest planet to the Sun, and it gets seven times the sunlight Earth does.
But it has almost no atmosphere. Just a thin exosphere. Nothing to hold the heat in, and nothing to breathe.
That is why the temperature swings are so violent. In sunlight the surface hits 430 degrees Celsius. At night it falls to minus 180.
NASA's latest suits are rated to 121 degrees. So in Mercury's daylight, you would cook inside your own suit.
Night is not much kinder. Those same suits give up at around minus 157.
And you cannot wait it out. One day and night on Mercury lasts 176 Earth days.
Your one real chance is the terminator zone. The thin band of twilight between day and night, where the temperature is actually survivable.
Land there in a working suit, and you last exactly as long as your oxygen does. A few hours.
Take the suit off, and Mercury is a vacuum. You would black out in about fifteen seconds, and be dead in under two minutes.
Venus.
Venus is the closest planet to Earth, and almost exactly Earth's size and gravity.
It is also the most hostile surface in the solar system.
On the way down you fall through clouds of sulfuric acid, so thick that only ten percent of the sunlight reaches the ground.
So it is dark down there. And it is 465 degrees. Hot enough to melt lead, everywhere on the planet, day and night.
Then there is the pressure. 92 bar, which is what you would feel 900 metres under Earth's ocean.
The toughest machine we ever put down there, the Soviet Venera 13, lasted 127 minutes.
You, in the best suit anyone has ever built, would get a few seconds before it failed.
Without one, you would be crushed, cooked and dissolved, in less than a second.
Mars.
Mars is the friendliest planet in the solar system, and that is not saying much.
On a summer afternoon at the equator it can reach a pleasant 20 degrees. That same night, it drops to minus 73.
The air is 95 percent carbon dioxide, with barely a trace of oxygen, and the pressure is under one percent of Earth's.
That matters more than the cold. Below six percent of Earth's pressure, the water in your body boils at your own body temperature. Mars sits well under that line.
So with no suit, Mars kills you the same way Mercury does. Unconscious in fifteen seconds, dead in under two minutes.
Put the suit on, and your problem becomes radiation. Fifty times the dose you would get on Earth, and it never stops.
The dust storms look worse than they are. The wind hits 100 kilometres an hour, but the air is so thin it feels like a breeze.
Give yourself a sealed, shielded habitat, and Mars finally stops being a countdown. You would last as long as your supplies do.
